decisions.quote: In replicating and extending Haun et al. (Experiment 1), English- but not Tseltal-speaking children could use their language-incongruent system when the instructions used their non-preferred frame of reference. Perseveration due to task order may explain the discrepancies between present English- and previous Dutch-speaking children, while not understanding task instructions using left/right language may explain why present Tseltal- and previous Hai||om-speaking children had difficulty with their language-incongruent systems.
decisions.reason: Whereas Haun et al. (2011) found that both Dutch- and Hai||om-speaking children had difficulty using their language-incongruent spatial reference frame, Experiment 1 replicated this difficulty for Tseltal-speaking children but found a discrepancy for English-speaking children, who could use their language-incongruent system. Because one comparison agrees with the original finding and the other explicitly diverges, the replication outcome is mixed.

parent_objection: First reply codes mixed across English versus original Dutch discrepancy and Tseltal versus Hai||om agreement. But abstract main conclusion says task constraints rather than language determine reference-frame performance; later experiments reproduce Tseltal ability when task instructions no longer use unfamiliar left/right language. Does this constitute main methodological-validity critique of original language-relative-hypothesis test, supporting statistically successful but flawed, or ordinary partial replication mixed with explanatory/extension experiments? Apply exact special-category rule: original effect obtained AND main argument method does not validly test hypothesis; cautious possible explanations alone not enough. Source is abstract-only. Explain whether original empirical effect recovered enough and critique is actually asserted as invalid-test main message, not just competing causal interpretation. Otherwise retain mixed or undeterminable with source scope.

shipped.title_o: Plasticity of human spatial cognition: Spatial language and cognition covary across cultures
shipped.outcome_quote: Although our results from the replication portion of the experiment mirrored those from Haun et al., data from our additional manipulations (counterbalancing the order of the egocentric and geocentric blocks for the English-speakers and as- sessing the Tseltal-speaking children’s left/right language comprehen- sion) did not favor the linguistic enculturation account.
